What's in 1.100.0 stable Never type Allocator API DropGuard API Conjuring zero-sized types Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo Reducing Cargo cache collisions Cargo min-publish-age Stabilized APIs Never type After 10 years and 5 failed stabilization attempts, the never type is finally stable ! This also completes the project goal for this work. The never type, spelled ! in code, is the canonical uninhabited type. It represents the type of diverging computations – computations which never resolve to any value – where any code that follows is unreachable. Expressions that terminate control flow, such as return , break , and std::process::exit , also have the type ! . Since having a value of the never type is impossible, Rust permits a never-to-any coercion, allowing to turn ! into any other type (this is what distinguishes it from any other uninhabited types). This can be used, for example, to not return a value from one of the branches of a match or an if : fn mrrrow ( option : Option < u32 > ) { let value = match option { // `x` has type `u32` Some ( x ) => x , // `return` has type `!`, which is then coerced to `u32`, // allowing the `match` to pass type checking. None => return , } ; // ... } While the never type could already be used and observed this way, and even named in the return type of functions ( -> ! ), this release allows naming the never type anywhere: fn infallible_unwrap < T > ( res : Result < T , ! > ) -> T { // ^^ writing `Result<_, !>` was not allowed before let Ok ( v ) = res ; v } Additionally this release changes Infallible to be an alias to the never type. That makes all old APIs that used Infallible be compatible with using ! . This was the plan ever since the introduction of Infallible and is one of the reasons why the never type stabilization was so hard (waffle gave a talk about some of the troubles of the stabilization). Unfortunately, to allow changing Infallible , we had to introduce a breaking change. This release changes the "never type fallback" from () to ! in editions before 2024 (i.e. 2015, 2018, and 2021), similarly to what has already been done in edition 2024 . This should largely be unnoticeable, but can affect code in some rare cases (for example when ignoring a result of a function returning a generic parameter). Note that this change might also make the compiler detect more code as unreachable. We tried to minimize the impact of this breaking change as much as possible, by providing future compatibility warnings far in advance and releasing fixes to public crates that have been broken by this. If a dependency is failing due to issues with the never type, consider updating it, as a fix might have already been released for it. Allocator API This release brings about the stabilization of the core parts of allocator_api , enabling library authors to define custom allocators that can be used together with certain standard library types - currently Vec and Box . These are enabled through the newly-stabilized Allocator trait. This is the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal . A lot remains to be done still, including expanding the API surface usable with custom allocators and stabilizing their use on more collections and pointer types; with the core trait and design out of the way though, expect to see more being stabilized soon! DropGuard : run a closure on every exit path The Drop trait in Rust makes it possible to run code when a variable goes out of scope, regardless of whether we return , ? , or panic. Drop being a part of types means that in Rust you never have to close a socket . Implementing Drop can however feel a little inconvenient when all you want is to run some code unconditionally when a function exits. This is why we’re introducing core::mem::DropGuard : a new helper type that runs a closure when dropped. DropGuard takes two arguments: a variable and a closure. It implements Deref and DerefMut so you can keep working with the variable as normal. But when dropped it runs the closure and consumes the variable. DropGuard also implements a dismiss method which returns the variable from the guard without running the destructor. This makes it possible to quickly implement all-or-nothing transaction-like APIs with a rollback. Here is an example implementing a parser which uses a guard to roll back mutations in case of failure: use std :: mem :: DropGuard ; use std :: num :: ParseIntError ; /// Attempt to parse all `strings` and push them into `nums`. /// If parsing any of them fails, `nums` remains unchanged. fn parse_all ( nums : & mut Vec < u32 > , strings : & [ & str ] ) -> Result < ( ) , ParseIntError > { let len = nums . len ( ) ; let mut nums = DropGuard :: new ( nums , move | nums | { nums . truncate ( len ) ; // ← 1. Reset the vec on failure } ) ; for s in strings { nums . push ( s . parse ( ) ? ) ; // ← 2. If `?` returns an error, roll back } DropGuard :: dismiss ( nums ) ; // ← 3. Parsing successful, dismiss the guard Ok ( ( ) ) } Conjuring zero-sized types As Rust's unsafe code guidelines are still being decided, it became clear that it would be very useful to decide what exactly it means to create zero-sized types in an unsafe way, and what we should recommend for people to do this. This question is answered in Rust 1.100 with a single function: std::mem::conjure_zst . Instead of transmuting () , MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init() , or various other incantations, this is the dedicated way to create a value of a zero-sized type when you know that doing so is safe to do. If an inhabited type has no size, we know exactly what value it must be: nothing. Of course, APIs often rely on the inability to construct such types for safety, and that's why this function is unsafe. For example, PyO3's Python<'py> is a zero-sized marker token that represents holding the Python GIL (global interpreter lock). Many of Python's APIs require holding this lock to be safe, but conjuring a token from thin air would allow safe PyO3 calls to violate that precondition. Reporting unused dependencies in Cargo Building dependencies that are no longer used or are only needed for specific platforms can slow down builds. Rustc has the unused_crate_dependencies lint for this but it has false positives when used with Cargo because dependencies may be shared between multiple build targets, e.g. dependencies.tracing-subscriber being available for every bin in a package when only some may use it. Cargo now reports unused dependencies to users, e.g. warning: unused dependency `tracing-subscriber` --> Cargo.toml:23:1 | 23 | tracing-subscriber.workspace = true | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ | = note: `cargo::unused_dependencies` is set to `warn` by default help: consider removing the dependency on `tracing-subscriber` A limitation of this warning is that it will only appear when building every build target that may use an entry in a dependencies table. For example, running cargo check --bin foo won't show warnings for unused [dependencies] because another bin may be present that uses them. No warning will be shown for unused dev-dependencies because there isn't a way to ensure every development build target is built. This warning is being introduced as part of a new linting system for Cargo, controlled by the [lints.cargo] table in Cargo.toml , completing this project goal . See also the other lints that have been introduced . Reducing Cargo cache collisions Cargo builds all libraries and binaries in the build-dir and then uplifts final artifacts to the target-dir . At this time, these share a common parent directory. Different build configurations, like --features , can lead to different copies of libraries and binaries in the build-dir . These copies are kept unique by a build-configuration hash but this hash was not always applied due to platform constraints. This can lead to extra rebuilds, missed rebuilds, confusion over what binaries or libraries are used, and so on. These problems get exacerbated when sharing a build-dir across git worktrees. The build-dir now consistently applies the build-configuration hash to all content by organizing the directories around their build step, rather than their file type, and moving the hash from a file's name to the parent directory. This work began with the build directory layout project goal in 2025, and its stabilization is a milestone toward a new project goal , unblocking future improvements such as cache garbage collection, cross-workspace cache de-duplication, cross-workspace caching, and fine grain locking. We previously published a call for testing for the changes that are now taking effect. While this is an internal change, this may break build processes and tests that had workarounds for missing or incomplete features. In some cases, the workaround is no longer needed. See cargo#17287 for possible solutions and to add any new use cases. Cargo min-publish-age a.k.a. dependency cooldowns Malicious versions of packages are often caught within hours or days after being published, by either automated scanners or by the community. Rust 1.100 stabilizes Cargo's min-publish-age aware dependency resolution, which lets you wait for that window before it picks up newly published versions. This practice is also known as dependency cooldowns. You can opt in via .cargo/config.toml : [ registry ] global-min-publish-age = " 3 days " When selecting versions, Cargo now skips any version published more recently than that, and tells you what it held back: $ cargo update Updating crates.io index Locking 2 packages to highest compatible version as of min-publish-age Adding cc v1.11.0 (available: v1.18.0, published 3 hours ago) Adding clap 4.6.7 (available: 4.6.9, published 2 days ago) When a new version is needed right away, you can override the check for a single update: $ CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_PUBLISH_AGE = a l l o w cargo update clap - -precise 4.6.9 Updating crates.io index Updating clap 4.6.7 -> clap 4.6.9 (published 2 days ago, minimum age 3 days) The newer version will be recorded in Cargo.lock and kept from then on until a later cargo update re-resolves it. A few things to keep in mind: This depends on the registry recording when each version was published. Versions without a pubtime field in the index are never held back. cargo install ignores the minimum publish age, for both the installed crate and its dependencies. Pin a version with cargo install foo@1.2.3 if needed. Cooldowns reduce the risk from some supply chain attacks but are not a complete defense on their own. Please keep reviewing dependency updates as you otherwise would. Further work to protect the ecosystem is planned under the crates.io supply chain hardening project goal , including quarantine support and automated detection of suspicious releases. items.summary: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. detail.findings_tradeoffs: Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues , where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments. items.headline: TTB: Test-time Baking for Efficient Rendering of Decoder-only View Synthesis Models
items.summary: Decoder-only Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) with KV-cache have recently achieved state-of-the-art quality by regressing novel views from neural networks without reconstructing 3D geometry, while Test-Time Training (TTT) layers save computation but sacrifice quality. We propose Test-Time Baking (TTB), a strategy that learns to bake global scene information from cross-view attention into a lightweight MLP, enabling fast and high-fidelity novel-view decoding. The first key is to repurpose the fast-weight MLP of TTT to learn the cross-view attention mapping explicitly from its input-output pairs, rather than replacing attention entirely, achieving the same rendering efficiency as TTT while delivering substantially higher quality.

items.headline: SO-Arena: Benchmarking the Capability Spectrum and Reliability of System One Models
items.summary: System One models promise fast, general-purpose decision-making without lengthy token generation. However, understanding their capability spectrum and decision reliability requires more than aggregate performance on current benchmarks. Existing evaluations often provide limited insight into the breadth of model capabilities and the reliability of their decisions.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: We introduce SO-Arena, a benchmark characterizing the capability spectrum and decision reliability of System One models across 11 domains and five capability families. For the capability spectrum, SO-Arena offers evidence-grounded evaluation through reliable sources and manual verification of reference labels against model-visible inputs; fine-grained capability assessment through domain-specific difficulty criteria; and realistic interactive evaluation, where models iteratively execute actions in sandboxes. Reasoning-intensive tasks further enable system one-two comparison. Beyond accuracy, SO-Arena assesses decision reliability through two complementary measures: decision stability under controlled option-set changes and missing-answer recognition when no valid option is available. Evaluations across 21 models reveal that the benefits of scaling and additional reasoning vary substantially across domains. More importantly, strong overall performance does not necessarily imply reliable decision-making: the best-performing System One model ranks only seventh in reliability. Together, these findings highlight the need to characterize capability spectrum and decision reliability as complementary dimensions, providing a systematic view of the strengths and limitations of System One models.

items.headline: G-STAR: Group-Scaled Token Capacity for Deeply Compressed Autoregressive Generation
items.summary: Discrete autoregressive models offer a scalable framework for image generation. However, they face a fundamental trade-off: long token sequences preserve representation quality but slow generation, while aggressive spatial compression reduces representation capacity. Based on product quantization, we show that, under a fixed nominal information budget, group size should scale quadratically with the per-axis spatial compression factor.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: Building on this principle, we propose GSTAR, a spatial--group co-scaling framework that enables $32\times$ and even effective $64\times$ compression while preserving strong reconstruction, understanding, and generation performance. Since larger groups introduce intra-group dependencies that must be modeled efficiently, we analyze their impact on inference latency and generation quality and introduce a semi-autoregressive decoder that combines parallel feature computation with lightweight causal modeling. With these designs, our highly compressed models perform competitively with leading models across five representative text-to-image benchmarks (GenEval, DPG-Bench, PRISM, LongText-Bench, and Qwen-Image-Bench). Together, these results show that highly compressed discrete representations can enable high-quality autoregressive generation at low latency.

items.headline: Duo: A Reciprocal World Model for Full-Duplex Interaction
items.summary: In this report, we introduce the Reciprocal World Model (RWM) and present Duo v1, a full-duplex world model that continuously perceives audiovisual inputs while responding to users in real time. The RWM treats intelligence and physical reality as equally fundamental to what constitutes a world. Existing world models largely focus on simulating the latter, leaving reasoning and decision-making as external controls rather than intrinsic parts of the world itself.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: In RWM, we identify two equally fundamental capabilities: Intent, which provides the cognition underlying world interactions, and Realization, which generates coherent audio-visual behavior. To realize this formulation, Duo v1 introduces three key technical designs: (1) Leveraging autoregressive modeling for continuous interaction reasoning and participation decisions, rather than restricting it to instruction understanding for diffusion models. (2) Constructing chunk-specific conditions and synchronize tokens across Intent and Realization on a unified timeline. Module-specific attention masks enforce causal dependencies both within and across chunks, preventing access to future inputs. (3) Mitigating distribution shift in both modules through dual rollout distillation, training on autoregressively generated Intent tokens and synthesized audiovisual histories from Realization. Both modules continuously perceive real-time audio, video, and text, enabling full-duplex interaction with spontaneous conversations and interruptions. Beyond conversation, users can share real objects, reshape virtual scenes, guide assistants, or play audiovisual games without mouse or keyboard controls. The release of Duo v1 makes our first step, with the next version coming soon. We look forward to broader exploration of this emerging field.

items.headline: PhysLoop: Harnessing LLMs' Physics Awareness for Self-Improving Video Generation Models
items.summary: Video generation models produce visually realistic videos but still struggle with physical dynamics and causal consistency. Learning from generated videos requires fine-grained physical supervision, yet reliable quality judgments, correction pairs, and controlled variations are difficult to obtain. Large language models (LLMs) possess physical knowledge, but struggle to reliably guide video generation models in producing their training videos.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: We present PhysLoop, a unified harness designed to support physically grounded self-improvement in video generation models. The harness guides and constrains LLMs throughout video generation, selection, and correction, distilling their physical knowledge into physically consistent videos. The framework supports controllable training-data construction and inference-time video repair. By identifying and correcting failures, PhysLoop marks a key milestone toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video generation models with limited human intervention. We release 100K videos spanning diverse, realistic indoor and outdoor scenes, along with generation tools and two evaluation datasets: PhysLoop-Gen and PhysLoop-Repair. We evaluate controllable generation and localized repair on these datasets, respectively, and assess physical behavior on the external Physics-IQ Verified benchmark.

items.headline: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents
items.summary: Decision models answer a question with a typed output, such as a choice among options with a probability for each, so one model can choose an agent's actions, evaluate actions already taken, or score every action to teach a policy with reinforcement learning. Prior work has studied them mainly as actors, judging their usefulness by how well they act. We ask whether a decision model that acts poorly can still teach well.

As actors, all six models are pulled away from a subgoal that must come first by an easier one. As judges that see the whole trajectory, the same models credit the steps toward that subgoal, and asking whether each action helped, rather than whether the task will succeed, separates useful from useless actions. As a teacher, JEV raises a Qwen2.5-1.5B policy over GRPO from 72.8% to 82.9% success on ALFWorld and from 56.8% to 71.4% on WebShop. These results suggest that a poor actor can still teach well, because judging an action after the episode ends reveals the consequences that acting must anticipate. Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/decision-agents.

items.headline: On the Design of Hyper-Connections: Simplification, Stability, and Scalability
items.summary: Hyper-Connections (HC) architectures are increasingly adopted in frontier language models, yet their components remain insufficiently understood and introduce non-negligible training overhead. In this work, we systematically study the HC architecture to understand its components and identify simpler, more efficient designs. We find that learned read/write gating without mixing and unconstrained mixing with fixed gates form two effective interaction groups: either alone achieves performance comparable to mHC.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: We present Open Vision Banana (OVB), a fully open and reproducible recipe for converting pretrained generators into unified multi-task perception systems. Our analyses identify the design choices that matter most for generalization, including color encoding, prompt design, parameter adaptation, and task balancing. These choices interact, so individually helpful choices can hurt when combined with others. Starting from 4B and 9B parameter open-weight base models and using 2.1M-3.8M training pairs from public datasets, OVB surpasses Vision Banana's reported Cityscapes zero-shot performance (73.9 vs. 69.9 mIoU) and rivals state-of-the-art affine-invariant depth estimators. Its non-zero-shot variants come within five points of Vision Banana on referring and reasoning segmentation but remain further behind on instance segmentation. All models largely retain the base model's image-editing abilities. With legend ensembling, we introduce a test-time scaling method for generator-based perception. It segments an image under several class-color legends and fuses the results by majority vote, correcting unstable color-class bindings and improving mIoU by up to 8.7 points on Cityscapes and 15.0 points on COCO-Object without retraining. We release the dataset construction and processing pipeline, the training and evaluation code, as well as the final, intermediate, and ablation checkpoints. Project website: https://openvisionbanana.github.io

items.headline: Accuracy Is Not Welfare: Evaluating AI Buyers under Strategic Price Complexity in a Synthetic Duopoly
items.summary: AI buying agents may alter sellers' incentives as well as consumers' decisions. In a synthetic duopoly, we evaluate price-comparison pipelines on a fixed menu and in empirical correlated-equilibrium games. Calculator assistance selects an optimal offer 84.00% of the time, versus 68.57% under verified-total disclosure, yet disclosure has a 20.14-unit higher consumer-worst equilibrium surplus.

detail.method_architecture: In antiferromagnets, light can also create correlated magnon pairs, or bimagnons. detail.findings_tradeoffs: Here we pump the phonon-assisted two-magnon absorption of NiO with mid-infrared pulses, far below its bandgap, and probe the resulting magnetic dynamics at finite momentum with time-resolved resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS). Upon photoexcitation, the one-magnon linewidth and energy are essentially unchanged, indicating that the long-range magnetic order is preserved without the photocarrier-induced demagnetization characteristic of above-bandgap excitation. A pump-induced two-magnon signal appears on the energy-gain (anti-Stokes) side of the spectrum. Its spectral weight peaks 4 ps after the pump, well beyond our 0.5 ps time resolution, indicative of a delayed growth likely due to momentum redistribution of the light-induced magnon pairs across the Brillouin zone. This two-magnon signal decays with a time constant of $28\pm11$ ps, exceeding the previously reported two-magnon dephasing time by more than two orders of magnitude. These results establish long-lived light-driven bimagnon correlations beyond the one-magnon state, akin to the higher-order correlations measured in ultracold gases.

items.headline: Verifiable Settlement and Pricing for Local Energy Markets: Architecture and Deployment on Hyperledger Besu
items.summary: We implement privacy-preserving local electricity exchanges using an automated market maker on the Hyperledger Besu network under QBFT consensus. The proposed protocol operator collects individual electricity positions off-chain and publishes aggregate supply and demand on the blockchain, where smart contracts compute market prices every fifteen minutes. Individual positions remain off-chain; Poseidon2 commitments and UltraHonk zeroknowledge proofs, generated from Noir circuits, verify aggregation, payments, and daily balance updates.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: Here is an example: Simple example: SYCL matrix multiply microbenchmark (Click for interactive SVG .) The green frames are the actual instructions running on the AI or GPU accelerator, aqua shows the source code for these functions, and red (C), yellow (C++), and orange (kernel) show the CPU code paths that initiated these AI/GPU programs. The gray "-" frames just help highlight the boundary between CPU and AI/GPU code. The x-axis is proportional to cost, so you look for the widest things and find ways to reduce them. Layers This flame graph shows a simple program for SYCL (a high-level C++ language for accelerators) that tests three implementations of matrix multiply, running them with the same input workload. The flame graph is dominated by the slowest implementation, multiply_basic(), which doesn't use any optimizations and consumes at 72% of stall samples and is shown as the widest tower. On the right are two thin towers for multiply_local_access() at 21% which replaces the accessor with a local variable, and multiply_local_access_and_tiling() at 6% which also adds matrix tiling. The towers are getting smaller as optimizations are added. This flame graph profiler is a prototype based on Intel EU stall profiling for hardware profiling and eBPF for software instrumentation. It's designed to be easy and low-overhead , just like a CPU profiler. You should be able to generate a flame graph of an existing AI workload whenever you want, without having to restart anything or launch additional code via an interposer. Instruction-offset Profiling This is not the first project to build an AI profiler or even something called an AI Flame Graph, however, others I've seen focus on tracing CPU stacks and timing accelerator execution, but don't profile the instruction offsets running on the accelerator; or do profile them but via expensive binary instrumentation. I wanted to build AI flame graphs that work like CPU flame graphs: Easy to use, negligible cost, production safe, and shows everything. A daily tool for developers, with most of the visualization in the language of the developer : source code functions. This has been an internal AI project at Intel for the past year. Intel was already investing in this space, building the EU stall profiler capability for the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series that provides an approximation of HW instruction sampling. I was lucky to have Dr. Matthew (Ben) Olson , an Intel AI engineer who has also worked on eBPF performance tooling ( processwatch ) as well as memory management research, join my team and do most of the development work. His background has helped us power through difficulties that seemed insurmountable. We've also recently been joined by Dr. Brandon Kammerdiener (coincidentally another graduate of the University of Tennessee, like Ben), who also has eBPF and memory internals experience, and has been helping us take on harder and harder workloads. And Gabriel Muñoz just joined today to help with releases. Now that our small team has shown that this is possible, we'll be joined by other teams at Intel to develop this further. We could have built a harder-to-use and higher-overhead version months ago using Intel GTPin but for widespread adoption it needs minimal overhead and ease of use so that developers don't hesitate to use this daily and to add it to deployment pipelines. What's a Flame Graph? A flame graph is a visualization I invented in 2011 for showing sampled code stack traces. It has become the standard for CPU profiling and analysis, helping developers quickly find performance improvements and eliminate regressions. A CPU flame graph shows the "big picture" of running software, with x-axis proportional to CPU cost. The example picture on the right summarizes how easy it can be to go from compute costs to responsible code paths. Prior to flame graphs, it could take hours to understand a complex profile by reading through hundreds of pages of output . Now it takes seconds: all you have to do is look for the widest rectangles. Flame graphs have had worldwide adoption. They have been the basis for five startups so far, have been adopted in over thirty performance analysis products, and have had over eighty implementations . My first implementation of flame graphs took a few hours on a Wednesday night after work. The real effort has been in the decade since, where I worked with different profilers, runtimes, libraries, kernels, compilers, and hypervisors to get flame graphs working properly in different environments, including fixing stack walking and symbolization. Earlier this year I posted about the final missing piece: Helping distros enable frame pointers so that profiling works across standard system libraries. Similar work is necessary for AI workloads: fixing stacks and symbols and getting profiling to work for different hardware, kernel drivers, user-mode drivers, frameworks, runtimes, languages, and models. A lot more work, too, as AI analysis has less maturity than CPU analysis. Searching Samples If you are new to flame graphs, it's worth mentioning the built-in search capability. In the earlier example, most of the stall samples are caused by sbid: software scoreboard dependency. As that may be a unique search term, you can run search (Ctrl-F, or click "Search") on "sbid" and it will highlight it in magenta: Search also shows the total number of stack samples that contained sbid in the bottom right: 78.4%. You can search for any term in the flame graph: accelerator instructions, source paths, function names, etc., to quickly calculate the percentage of stacks where it is present (excluding vertical overlap) helping you prioritise performance work. Note that the samples are EU stall-based, which means theoretical performance wins can take the percentages down to zero. This is different to timer-based samples as are typically used in CPU profiling. Stalls mean you better focus on the pain, the parts of the code that aren't making forward progress, but you aren't seeing resource usage by unstalled instructions. I'd like to supuport timer-based samples in the future as well, so we can have both views. Who will use this? At a recent golang conference, I asked the audience of 200+ to raise their hands if they were using CPU flame graphs. Almost every hand went up. I know of companies where flame graphs are a daily tool that developers use to understand and tune their code, reducing compute costs. This will become a daily tool for AI developers. My employer will use this as well for evaluation analysis, to find areas to tune to beat competitors, as well as to better understand workload performance to aid design. Why is AI profiling hard? Consider CPU instruction profiling: This is easy when the program and symbol table are both in the file system and in a standardized file format (such as ELF) as is the case with native compiled code (C). CPU profiling gets hard for JIT-complied code, like Java, as instructions and symbols are dynamically generated and placed in main memory (the process heap) without following a universal standard. For such JITted code we use runtime-specific methods and agents to retrieve snapshots of the heap information, which is different for each runtime. AI workloads also have different runtimes (and frameworks, languages, user-mode drivers, compilers, etc.) any of which can require special tinkering to get their CPU stacks and symbols to work. These CPU stacks are shown as the red, orange, and yellow frames in the AI Flame Graph. Some AI workloads are easy to get these frames working, some (like PyTorch) are a lot more work. But the real challenge is instruction profiling of actual GPU and AI accelerator programs -- shown as the aqua and green frames -- and correctly associating them with the CPU stacks beneath them. Not only may these GPU and AI programs not exist in the file system, but they may not even exist in main memory! Even for running programs. Once execution begins, they may be deallocated from main memory and only exist in special accelerator memory, beyond the direct reach of OS profilers and debuggers. Or within reach, but only through a prohibitively high-overhead HW-specific debugger interface. There's also no /proc representation for these programs either (I've been proposing building an equivalent) so there's no direct way to even tell what is running and what isn't, and all the other /proc details. Forget instruction profiling, even ps(1) and all the other process tools do not work. It's been a mind-bending experience, revealing what gets taken for granted because it has existed in CPU land for decades: A process table. Process tools. Standard file formats. Programs that exist in the file system. Programs running from main memory. Debuggers. Profiliers. Core dumping. Disassembling. Single stepping. Static and dynamic instrumentation. Etc. For GPUs and AI, this is all far less mature. It can make the work exciting at times, when you think something is impossible and then find or devise a way. Fortunately we have a head start as some things do exist. Depending on the runtime and kernel driver, there are debug interfaces where you can list running accelerator programs and other statistics, as used by tools like intel_gpu_top(1). You can kill -9 a GPU workload using intel_gpu_abrt(1). Some interfaces can even generate basic ELF files for the running accelerator programs that you can try to load in a debugger like gdb(1). And there is support for GPU/AI program disassembly, if you can get your hands on the binary. It feels to me like GPU/AI debugging, OS style, is about two years old. Better than zero, but still early on, and lots more ahead of us. A decade, at least. What do AI developers think of this? We've shown AI Flame Graphs to other AI developers at Intel and a common reaction is to be a bit puzzled, wondering what to do with it. AI developers think about their bit of code, but with AI Flame Graphs they can now see the entire stack for the first time, including the HW, and many layers they don't usually think about or don't know about. It basically looks like a pile of gibberish with their code only a small part of the flame graph. CPU Flame Graph Implementations This reaction is similar to people's first experiences with CPU flame graphs, which show parts of the system that developers and engineers typically don't work on, such as runtime internals, system libraries, and kernel internals. Flame graphs are great at highlighting the dozen or so functions that matter the most, so it becomes a problem of learning what those functions do across a few different code bases, which are typically open source. Understanding a dozen such functions can take a few hours or even a few days -- but if this leads to a 10% or 2x cost win, it is time well spent. And the next time the user looks at a flame graph, they start saying "I've seen that function before" and so on. You can get to the point where understanding the bulk of a CPU flame graph takes less than a minute: look for the widest tower, click to zoom, read the frames, done. I'm encouraged by the success of CPU flame graphs, with over 80 implementations and countless real world case studies. Sometimes I'm browsing a performance issue I care about on github and hit page down and there's a CPU flame graph. They are everywhere. I expect AI developers will also be able to understand AI Flame Graphs in less than a minute, but to start with people will be spending a day or more browsing code bases they didn't know were involved. Publishing case studies of found wins will also help people learn how to interpret them, and also help explain the value. What about PyTorch? Another common reaction we've had is that AI developers are using PyTorch, and initially we didn't support it as it meant walking Python stacks, which isn't trivial. But prior work has been done there (to support CPU profiling) and after a lot of tinkering we now have the first PyTorch AI Flame Graph: PyTorch frames in pink (Click for interactive SVG .) The PyTorch functions are at the bottom and are colored pink. This example runs oneDNN kernels that are JIT-generated, and don't have a source path so that layer just reads "jit". Getting all other the layers included was a real pain to get going, but an important milestone. We think if we can do PyTorch we can do anything. In this flame graph, we show PyTorch running the Llama 2 7B model using the Intel Extensions for PyTorch (IPEX). This flame graph shows the origin of the GPU kernel execution all the way back to the Python source code shown in pink. Most samples are from a stack leading up to a gemm_kernel (matrix multiply) shown in aqua, which like the previous example has many stalls due to software scoreboarding. There are two instructions (0xa30 and 0xa90) that combined are 27% of the entire profile. I expect someone will ask: Can't we just click on instructions and have it bring up a dissassembly view with full source? Yes, that should be possible, but I can't answer how we're going to provide this yet. Another expected question I can't yet answer: Since there are now multiple products providing AI auto-tuning of CPU workloads using CPU flame graphs (including Intel Granulate ) can't we have AI auto-tuning of AI workloads using AI Flame Graphs? First Release: Sometimes hard and with moderate overhead Getting AI Flame Graphs to work with some workloads is easy, but others are currently hard and cost moderate overhead. It's similar to CPU profiling, where some workloads and languages are easy to profile, whereas others need various things fixed. Some AI workloads use many software dependencies that need various tweaks and recompilation (e.g., enabling frame pointers so that stack walking works) making setup time consuming. PyTorch is especially difficult and can take over a week of OS work to be ready for AI Flame Graphs. We will work on getting these tweaks changed upstream in their respective repositories, something involving teams inside and outside of Intel, and is a process I'd expect to take at least a year. During that time AI workloads will gradually become easier to flame graph, and with lower-overhead as well. I'm reminded of eBPF in the early days: You had to patch and recompile the kernel and LLVM and Clang, which could take multiple days if you hit errors. Since then all the eBPF dependency patches have been merged, and default settings changed, so that eBPF "just works." We'll get there with AI Flame Graphs too, but right now it's still those early days. The changes necessary for AI Flame Graphs are really about improving debugging in general, and are a requirement for Fast by Friday : A vision where we can root-cause analyze anything in five days or less. Availability AI Flame Graphs will first become available on the Intel Tiber AI Cloud as a preview feature for the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series. If you are currently deployed there you can ask through the Intel service channel for early access. As for if or when it will support other hardware types, be in other Intel products, be officially launched, be open source, etc., these involve various other teams at Intel and they need to make their own announcements before I can discuss them here. Conclusions Finding performance improvements for AI data centers of just fractions of a percent can add up to planetary savings in electricity, water, and money. If AI flame graphs have the success that CPU flame graphs have had, I'd expect finding improvements of over 10% will be common, and 50% and higher will eventually be found*. But it won't be easy in these early days as there are still many software components to tweak and recompile, and software layers to learn about that are revealed in the AI flame graph. In the years ahead I imagine others will build their own AI flame graphs that look the same as this one, and there may even be startups selling them, but if they use more difficult-to-use and higher-overhead technologies I fear they could turn companies off the idea of AI flame graphs altogether and prevent them from finding sorely needed wins. This is too important to do badly. AI flame graphs should be easy to use, cost negligible overhead, be production safe, and show everything. Intel has proven it's possible. Disclaimer * This is a personal blog post that makes personal predictions but not guarantees of possible performance improvements. Feel free to take any claim with a grain of salt, and feel free to wait for an official publication and public launch by Intel on this technology. 1 Based on halving the Arm CEO Rene Haas' estimate of 20-25% quoted in Taking a closer look at AI's supposed energy apocalypse by Kyle Orland of ArsTechnica. Updates (Jan 2025): I wasn't going to talk about other specific profilers, but since FAQ #1 is "what about NVIDIA?": They do have flame graphs in Nsight Graphics for GPU workloads, so I'd guess they aren't far from supporting AI workloads as well. Their version looks shallow as it's only the GPU code, so it is missing the CPU context necessary to understand the full picture, and seems based on interposing (launching the app from Nsights) which is the old method. The new method we've created allows for easy, everything, anytime profiling, like you expect from CPU profilers. Theirs does have click-to-source integration, which is quite handy, and I do like the default orientation and colors, thank you! Thanks Thanks to everyone at Intel who have helped us make this happen. Markus Flierl has driven this project and made it a top priority, and Greg Lavender has expressed his support. Special thanks to Michael Cole, Matthew Roper, Luis Strano, Rodrigo Vivi, Joonas Lahtinen, Stanley Gambarin, Timothy Bauer, Brandon Yates, Maria Kraynyuk, Denis Samoylov, Krzysztof Raszkowski, Sanchit Jain, Po-Yu Chen, Felix Degrood, Piotr Rozenfeld, Andi Kleen, and all of the other coworkers that helped clear things up for us, and thanks in advance for everyone else who will be helping us in the months ahead. My final thanks is to the companies and developers who do the actual hands-on work with flame graphs, collecting them, examining them, finding performance wins, and applying them. You are helping save the planet.

My employer will use this as well for evaluation analysis, to find areas to tune to beat competitors, as well as to better understand workload performance to aid design. Why is AI profiling hard? Consider CPU instruction profiling: This is easy when the program and symbol table are both in the file system and in a standardized file format (such as ELF) as is the case with native compiled code (C). CPU profiling gets hard for JIT-complied code, like Java, as instructions and symbols are dynamically generated and placed in main memory (the process heap) without following a universal standard. For such JITted code we use runtime-specific methods and agents to retrieve snapshots of the heap information, which is different for each runtime. AI workloads also have different runtimes (and frameworks, languages, user-mode drivers, compilers, etc.) any of which can require special tinkering to get their CPU stacks and symbols to work. These CPU stacks are shown as the red, orange, and yellow frames in the AI Flame Graph. Some AI workloads are easy to get these frames working, some (like PyTorch) are a lot more work. But the real challenge is instruction profiling of actual GPU and AI accelerator programs -- shown as the aqua and green frames -- and correctly associating them with the CPU stacks beneath them. Not only may these GPU and AI programs not exist in the file system, but they may not even exist in main memory! Even for running programs. Once execution begins, they may be deallocated from main memory and only exist in special accelerator memory, beyond the direct reach of OS profilers and debuggers. Or within reach, but only through a prohibitively high-overhead HW-specific debugger interface. There's also no /proc representation for these programs either (I've been proposing building an equivalent) so there's no direct way to even tell what is running and what isn't, and all the other /proc details. Forget instruction profiling, even ps(1) and all the other process tools do not work. It's been a mind-bending experience, revealing what gets taken for granted because it has existed in CPU land for decades: A process table. Process tools. Standard file formats. Programs that exist in the file system. Programs running from main memory. Debuggers. Profiliers. Core dumping. Disassembling. Single stepping. Static and dynamic instrumentation. Etc. For GPUs and AI, this is all far less mature. It can make the work exciting at times, when you think something is impossible and then find or devise a way. Fortunately we have a head start as some things do exist. Depending on the runtime and kernel driver, there are debug interfaces where you can list running accelerator programs and other statistics, as used by tools like intel_gpu_top(1). You can kill -9 a GPU workload using intel_gpu_abrt(1). Some interfaces can even generate basic ELF files for the running accelerator programs that you can try to load in a debugger like gdb(1). And there is support for GPU/AI program disassembly, if you can get your hands on the binary. It feels to me like GPU/AI debugging, OS style, is about two years old. Better than zero, but still early on, and lots more ahead of us. A decade, at least. What do AI developers think of this? We've shown AI Flame Graphs to other AI developers at Intel and a common reaction is to be a bit puzzled, wondering what to do with it. AI developers think about their bit of code, but with AI Flame Graphs they can now see the entire stack for the first time, including the HW, and many layers they don't usually think about or don't know about. It basically looks like a pile of gibberish with their code only a small part of the flame graph. CPU Flame Graph Implementations This reaction is similar to people's first experiences with CPU flame graphs, which show parts of the system that developers and engineers typically don't work on, such as runtime internals, system libraries, and kernel internals. Flame graphs are great at highlighting the dozen or so functions that matter the most, so it becomes a problem of learning what those functions do across a few different code bases, which are typically open source. Understanding a dozen such functions can take a few hours or even a few days -- but if this leads to a 10% or 2x cost win, it is time well spent. And the next time the user looks at a flame graph, they start saying "I've seen that function before" and so on. You can get to the point where understanding the bulk of a CPU flame graph takes less than a minute: look for the widest tower, click to zoom, read the frames, done. I'm encouraged by the success of CPU flame graphs, with over 80 implementations and countless real world case studies. Sometimes I'm browsing a performance issue I care about on github and hit page down and there's a CPU flame graph. They are everywhere. I expect AI developers will also be able to understand AI Flame Graphs in less than a minute, but to start with people will be spending a day or more browsing code bases they didn't know were involved. Publishing case studies of found wins will also help people learn how to interpret them, and also help explain the value. What about PyTorch? Another common reaction we've had is that AI developers are using PyTorch, and initially we didn't support it as it meant walking Python stacks, which isn't trivial. But prior work has been done there (to support CPU profiling) and after a lot of tinkering we now have the first PyTorch AI Flame Graph: PyTorch frames in pink (Click for interactive SVG .) The PyTorch functions are at the bottom and are colored pink. This example runs oneDNN kernels that are JIT-generated, and don't have a source path so that layer just reads "jit". Getting all other the layers included was a real pain to get going, but an important milestone. We think if we can do PyTorch we can do anything. In this flame graph, we show PyTorch running the Llama 2 7B model using the Intel Extensions for PyTorch (IPEX). This flame graph shows the origin of the GPU kernel execution all the way back to the Python source code shown in pink. Most samples are from a stack leading up to a gemm_kernel (matrix multiply) shown in aqua, which like the previous example has many stalls due to software scoreboarding. There are two instructions (0xa30 and 0xa90) that combined are 27% of the entire profile. I expect someone will ask: Can't we just click on instructions and have it bring up a dissassembly view with full source? Yes, that should be possible, but I can't answer how we're going to provide this yet. Another expected question I can't yet answer: Since there are now multiple products providing AI auto-tuning of CPU workloads using CPU flame graphs (including Intel Granulate ) can't we have AI auto-tuning of AI workloads using AI Flame Graphs? First Release: Sometimes hard and with moderate overhead Getting AI Flame Graphs to work with some workloads is easy, but others are currently hard and cost moderate overhead. It's similar to CPU profiling, where some workloads and languages are easy to profile, whereas others need various things fixed. Some AI workloads use many software dependencies that need various tweaks and recompilation (e.g., enabling frame pointers so that stack walking works) making setup time consuming. PyTorch is especially difficult and can take over a week of OS work to be ready for AI Flame Graphs. We will work on getting these tweaks changed upstream in their respective repositories, something involving teams inside and outside of Intel, and is a process I'd expect to take at least a year. During that time AI workloads will gradually become easier to flame graph, and with lower-overhead as well. I'm reminded of eBPF in the early days: You had to patch and recompile the kernel and LLVM and Clang, which could take multiple days if you hit errors. Since then all the eBPF dependency patches have been merged, and default settings changed, so that eBPF "just works." We'll get there with AI Flame Graphs too, but right now it's still those early days. The changes necessary for AI Flame Graphs are really about improving debugging in general, and are a requirement for Fast by Friday : A vision where we can root-cause analyze anything in five days or less. Availability AI Flame Graphs will first become available on the Intel Tiber AI Cloud as a preview feature for the Intel Data Center GPU Max Series. If you are currently deployed there you can ask through the Intel service channel for early access. As for if or when it will support other hardware types, be in other Intel products, be officially launched, be open source, etc., these involve various other teams at Intel and they need to make their own announcements before I can discuss them here. Conclusions Finding performance improvements for AI data centers of just fractions of a percent can add up to planetary savings in electricity, water, and money. If AI flame graphs have the success that CPU flame graphs have had, I'd expect finding improvements of over 10% will be common, and 50% and higher will eventually be found*. But it won't be easy in these early days as there are still many software components to tweak and recompile, and software layers to learn about that are revealed in the AI flame graph. In the years ahead I imagine others will build their own AI flame graphs that look the same as this one, and there may even be startups selling them, but if they use more difficult-to-use and higher-overhead technologies I fear they could turn companies off the idea of AI flame graphs altogether and prevent them from finding sorely needed wins. This is too important to do badly. AI flame graphs should be easy to use, cost negligible overhead, be production safe, and show everything. Intel has proven it's possible. Feel free to take any claim with a grain of salt, and feel free to wait for an official publication and public launch by Intel on this technology. 1 Based on halving the Arm CEO Rene Haas' estimate of 20-25% quoted in Taking a closer look at AI's supposed energy apocalypse by Kyle Orland of ArsTechnica. Their version looks shallow as it's only the GPU code, so it is missing the CPU context necessary to understand the full picture, and seems based on interposing (launching the app from Nsights) which is the old method. The new method we've created allows for easy, everything, anytime profiling, like you expect from CPU profilers. Theirs does have click-to-source integration, which is quite handy, and I do like the default orientation and colors, thank you! items.headline: Toward the abelian category of positive Lagrangians
items.summary: We introduce a geometric construction whose terminal configuration determines the kernel and cokernel of a morphism between positive Lagrangian branes in the derived Fukaya category of a Calabi-Yau manifold. Thus, if the construction always terminates, the full subcategory of positive Lagrangian branes is abelian, as conjectured by Joyce. We show that this abelian category admits Harder-Narasimhan filtrations with respect to the central charge defined by the holomorphic volume form.

items.summary: Kalah is a classic two-player game in the mancala family of sowing games. We study the natural generalization in which the number of pits per side is part of the input and an arbitrary position is given, with the stone counts given in unary.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: We show that deciding whether a designated player can force a win from such a position is PSPACE-complete. The hard positions have Alice to move first and both stores initially empty. The same positions are hard under either common convention for capture opposite an empty pit, and with or without the bonus rule, which gives a player another turn when the last stone is sown into their own store. We introduce Line Kalah as an intermediate problem, a game on a line in which stones that leave the line effectively disappear and Alice must save each of her target pits before Bob captures it, and we reduce quantified Boolean formulas to it. Finally, the line positions are embedded in Kalah with both stores empty. A separate Bob pit holds the score adjustment, so the winner takes a strict majority of the stones.

items.headline: Dimension drop for superlevel sets of the uniform Littlewood constant
items.summary: For $(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ and $Q\ge 1$, set $F_Q(x,y)=Q\min_{1\le q\le Q}\lVert qx\rVert\lVert qy\rVert$, where $q$ ranges over positive integers and $\lVert\cdot\rVert$ denotes distance to the nearest integer. The set on which the uniform Littlewood constant $L=\limsup_{Q\to\infty}F_Q$ is positive has full Hausdorff dimension. We prove that for every fixed $c>0$ the superlevel set $\{L\ge c\}$ has Hausdorff dimension strictly less than two.

items.headline: Learning Dynamics of the Influencer's Game in Resource Landscapes
items.summary: Across domains as varied as ecology, economics, and online platforms, individuals are incentivized to position themselves within resource-rich strategy spaces. In this work we introduce a new spatial game framework called the influencer's game. Within this new framework players' strategies are represented as positions within a trait space.

For the influencer's game, we show that there is a unique symmetric Nash equilibrium that exists under strict log-concavity of the influence kernel. Using the unique equilibrium we show that the stability of the system depends on the influence kernel's parameters, number of players, and the resource distribution shape. For any dimension we demonstrate a stability threshold that depends on both the scatter and curvature of the players. When this threshold is crossed, the symmetric equilibrium destabilizes and gives way to a variety of bifurcation types; including, specialist clusters, limit cycles, and sub-games that reproduce the larger game's structure. We ground these results using real-world data for resources as a demonstration of the game's application. Finally we extend the game dynamics to use multi-agent reinforcement learning and further show that the predicted bifurcation structure persists under partial observability and discretized strategy spaces. In all, the influencer's game provides a novel framework for predicting when competitive pressure drives convergence versus fragmentation with possible applications across domains.

items.summary: Research on pay dispersion has long asked whether unequal rewards increase or depress performance. Tournament theory expects stronger effort, while social comparison accounts expect withdrawal. Both perspectives, however, treat performance as a single scale on which workers can be ranked.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: Scientific work often resists such ordering. Some contributions extend recognized lines of inquiry and can be evaluated against prevailing standards; others revise the frames through which value is judged and become legible only later. We argue that intellectual tournaments more readily reward the first kind of contribution than the second. Pay dispersion may therefore be associated not only with how much scholars produce but also with what kinds of intellectual exploration are encouraged. We test this argument with administrative payroll records for 105,050 tenure-line faculty in 4,839 departments at 93 U.S. public universities from 2004 to 2026, linked to publication histories in OpenAlex. For each department, we estimate a separate pay equation using rank, contract basis, and seniority, then measure the Gini of the salary variation this local ladder cannot explain. Scholars in departments with greater unexplained pay dispersion publish more papers and receive more citations, but their work is less disruptive, less novel, and more conventional. Additional analyses show that compensation premiums above the ladder go disproportionately to scholars with broad collaborations and topical breadth. Although the design cannot fully separate treatment from selection, the evidence shows that inequality is not only a distributional outcome but also an evaluative structure, shaping which forms of knowledge are recognized, rewarded, and reproduced within organizations and communities.

items.headline: Designing Information in a Forest: Algorithmic Aspects. The Bayesian persuasion framework models strategic information revelation by a sender to one or more receivers.
items.summary: The Bayesian persuasion framework models strategic information revelation by a sender to one or more receivers. We study an intricate version of the multi-receiver persuasion setting in which the communication hierarchy is a forest - i.e., some receivers observe more informative signals than others, and the partial ordering of the receivers according to the information they get is represented by a pre-specified directed forest. This model naturally captures interactions in hierarchical organizations, and it lies in between the two most commonly studied versions of Bayesian persuasion: private persuasion and public persuasion.

items.headline: A deployed four-city entanglement-based QKD network with real-time key delivery, benchmarked against finite-key security bounds
items.summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) generates shared secret keys whose security rests on the laws of physics rather than on computational assumptions. We report the entanglement-based segment of the Slovak national quantum communication infrastructure, connecting four cities in western Slovakia over deployed telecommunication fiber. items.headline: Implementation of a 1D Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD under finite-size parameter estimation
items.summary: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) is a promising technology for quantum-secure communications, offering high secret-key rates and straightforward integration with coherent optical communication systems. Conventional Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD encodes information in both optical-field quadratures, increasing requirements for state preparation, modulation, and calibration, while potentially introducing additional preparation imperfections. Unidimensional (1D) Gaussian modulation offers a simpler alternative by encoding information in only one quadrature, while the conjugate quadrature constrains the protocol's security.

items.headline: Lattice response theory for subsystem symmetry-protected topological phases
items.summary: We develop a framework to study subsystem symmetry-protected topological (SSPT) phases using lattice response theory. We begin with a systematic construction of spacetime lattice gauge fields from general microscopic $X$-type symmetry actions on qudit systems, including global symmetries, subsystem symmetries, and more general modulated symmetries. Given a gauge-invariant response action, we then construct a corresponding entangler and explicitly show that it implements stacking with the SSPT phase described by the response action.

items.headline: Fictitious Play When Agents Are Not Expected-Utility Maximizers: A Geometric Analysis in $2$-Action Games
items.summary: Fictitious play (FP) is one of the earliest and most fundamental learning procedures in games, where each agent independently chooses a best response to the empirical distribution of opponents' past actions by maximizing the expected payoff with respect to it. However, learning agents may not always be expected-utility maximizers: they may use nonlinear evaluation functionals to account for the uncertainty induced by the opponents, e.g., via risk measures. In this work, we study nonlinear fictitious play (NL-FP), in which each pure action is evaluated by a general, possibly nonlinear functional of the payoff distribution induced by the opponent's empirical belief.

items.headline: Structure-Preserving Leaky Integrate-and-Fire Dynamics on Arbitrary Time Scales
items.summary: The leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron combines a passive membrane law with threshold-triggered firing and reset. We formulate this hybrid neuron model, under constant input, on an arbitrary Hilger time scale $\mathbb{T}$. Our central result is that, after the first spike, the firing times satisfy $t_{n+1}=Π_{\mathbb{T}}^{+}(t_n+T_c)$, where $T_c$ is the classical reset-to-threshold travel time.

items.headline: Infrastructure for Verifiable AI: Where Proof Costs Go and How Hardware Can Help
items.summary: Users of artificial intelligence services, including those powered by large language models and other transformer-based models, need assurance that inference and training follow the declared computation without exposing private models or data. Zero-knowledge proofs can provide this assurance, but proof generation remains expensive. Hardware acceleration research often reports gains for individual cryptographic operations, leaving their effect on the full cost of proving neural-network workloads, particularly large transformer models, unclear.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: We introduce a four-layer framework linking verifiable AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware platforms, use it to review the literature, and add original measurements of six provers and seven kernels to identify which costs matter in practice. Our measurements show that the dominant cost changes with the proof system and input length. In low-rank fine-tuning, the cost of opening commitments to fixed model weights remains nearly constant across input lengths from 64 to 2048, while the work associated with intermediate values grows. A 13-billion-parameter fine-tuning configuration exceeds the capacity of a 40-gigabyte graphics processor but completes on an 80-gigabyte device, showing why capacity must be assessed alongside execution time. We use these findings to assess graphics processors, reconfigurable logic, custom chips and existing artificial intelligence accelerators. The resulting research agenda connects proof-friendly numeric formats, reuse of fixed-weight commitments, heterogeneous execution and shared benchmarks to the measured bottlenecks. Effective acceleration requires selecting hardware and proof-system optimizations around the cost profile of the target workload.

items.headline: What Does It Cost to Force-Close a Lightning Channel? Evidence from 974,000 Channel Closes, 2018-2026
items.summary: Bitcoin's Lightning payment network returns the funds of a channel that cannot close cooperatively through pre-signed transactions whose fees and delays fall on its operators. That fee design is being replaced: Bitcoin Core 31.0 removed the mempool rule anchor channels relied on, and the Lightning specification adopted zero-fee commitments in May 2026. What the old design costs has never been measured across fee regimes.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: We trace every public channel close and every force close on-chain from January 2018 to October 2026, 973,581 closes, and follow each output to its spend. A separate chain index confirms all 698,476 public closes we could compare. Fee spikes did not bring a wave of force closes. Force closes in a spike week and the next were 0.97 times the four weeks before, against 1.02 after ordinary weeks of the same years. A force close costs 2-6 times a cooperative close in fees and locks the closer's balance for days, which outweighs the fees only in low-fee years. When fees are high, pending payments are exposed: in 2023, 18.2% of HTLC timeouts confirmed more than 40 blocks after expiry. Yet since 2021, forwarding nodes lost only 38 payments, each with the preimage already on-chain. Anchor outputs cut late timeouts in fee spikes (20.6% against 30.5%), yet owners rarely bump commitments with them, and miners take most of what third parties sweep. Zero-fee commitments would save only 12% of the anchor mechanism's block space; they should be judged by how promptly payments resolve when fees spike.

items.summary: Summary: Identifying epigenetically modified bases (e.g., methylation) is crucial for many important applications such as discovering mechanisms of cancer development, cell differentiation, and bacterial defense. Nanopore sequencing generates electrical signals that can differentiate canonical bases from modified ones. To detect base modifications from signals, machine learning (ML) methods and statistical approaches are commonly used.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: These methods can either detect a specific modification type or require an additional unmodified copy of the same DNA as a control group. However, no released model detects modification types beyond those it was trained for, which makes it difficult to detect rare modification types without an unmodified control. Our goal is to accurately identify the presence of modified sites regardless of their modification type, which we define as modification-agnostic detection. To this end, we propose RawMod, a transformer-based modification-agnostic and control-free method for detecting epigenetically modified genomic positions. The key idea of RawMod is to compare the raw signals of many reads at each site with the unmodified reference sequence, using a small model that learns many modification types as a single modified class. Based on our extensive evaluations on the detection of various modification types (5mC, 5hmC, 4mC, 6mA, and 5hmU) using various genomes, RawMod achieves the highest mean AUROC across modifications compared to control-based methods and control-free modification models. A single RawMod model with 0.23M parameters detects five modification types with a mean AUROC of 0.964, against 0.799 for the best released model. When a modification type is withheld from training, RawMod still detects it (AUROC 0.91--0.98), provided another modification of the same base was seen in training. We use RawMod to map 5hmU without a control across a 7.7 Mb contig of the Amphidinium carterae genome, consistent with two published trends. Further, we show that the modification-aware embeddings from RawMod can be used to differentiate read origin (e.g., cell types, tumor/normal origin, and native/PCR-amplified DNA). We discuss how RawMod can enable further work on label-free classification of cell types using these modification-aware embeddings. Availability and Implementation: RawMod is available at https://github.com/STORMgroup/RawMod and at https://huggingface.co/STORMResearch/RawMod. We also provide the scripts to fully reproduce our results on our GitHub page and release our datasets on SquiDBase.

items.headline: The Confessions of a Protein Language Model: Steering, Activations, and What Predicted Confidence Cannot Certify
items.summary: Protein generate-and-screen pipelines use interventions and readouts to select candidates, but rarely test whether these track their intended targets. We audit published repetition steering, ESMFold confidence, and an activation readout. Steering preserves confidence at its operating point, but a fitted cliff follows at alpha_50 = 1.240x (sweep's own control: 64.0%).

items.summary: Matching statistics and supermaximal exact matches (SMEMs) are key inputs for sequence homology search and classification. Methods such as MONI, PHONI, and ropebwt3 compute these statistics using compressed pangenome indexes, but are substantially slower than methods that compute approximations of matching statistics, such as pseudo-matching lengths (PMLs). PMLs can be computed quickly in a single pass, but SMEM computation can require overlapping forward or backward passes over the query.

items.headline: scDeepSim: Deep Generative Simulation for Controlled Benchmarking of Single-Cell Methods
items.summary: Benchmarking single-cell computational methods requires both realistic data and reliable ground truth. However, annotating real datasets is costly and, even when available, may not fully represent the diverse settings where methods are used. Simulators address this gap by generating synthetic data that has fully specified ground truth and whose structure can be tailored to challenge competing methods.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: Existing single-cell simulators can broadly be divided into statistical and deep generative classes. Statistical simulators offer interpretable parameters for controlling simulated data, but their modeling assumptions may not accurately represent real data. Deep generative models can learn complex expression patterns, but it remains unclear how to transparently control individual biological or technical factors without introducing unintended effects. We introduce scDeepSim, a simulator that combines a structured variational autoencoder with latent diffusion to generate synthetic single-cell expression profiles. It allows users to intervene on selected biological or technical factors at user-specified strengths, producing realistic datasets with benchmark ground truth. We demonstrate this capability by benchmarking batch correction and trajectory inference methods, showing how batch-effect strength affects batch mixing and cell-type preservation, and how trajectory geometry and noise affect pseudotime recovery. scDeepSim therefore enables researchers to vary selected biological and technical factors in realistic simulated data and assess how these changes affect the performance of single-cell analysis methods, helping understand when such methods may be appropriately applied. Code for the scDeepSim simulator and experiments is available at https://github.com/LangtianM/scDeepSim.

items.headline: RNA Small-Molecule Binding-Site Prediction by Integrating RNA Language Models and Structural Geometry
items.summary: RNAs are emerging as promising therapeutic targets, and small-molecule binding can modulate their structure and function, creating opportunities for therapeutic development. Accurate identification of RNA small-molecule binding sites is therefore important for understanding RNA-ligand interactions and facilitating RNA-targeted drug discovery. However, the structural complexity of RNA and the limited availability of experimentally characterized RNA-ligand complexes pose challenges for computational binding-site prediction.

The model integrates geometric descriptors of the local three-dimensional environment with pretrained RNA language model embeddings to capture complementary structural and sequence information. We investigate three pretrained RNA language models RNA-BERT, ERNIE-RNA and RNA-FM and assess the contributions of sequence representations and geometric features through feature-level ablation experiments. The model is developed using the TR60 and HARIBOSS datasets and evaluated on four independent benchmark datasets: RB9, TE18, TL12 and JL10. RSMBind achieves the highest MCC among the compared methods on three of the four benchmarks, with relative improvements of 17.1% on RB9, 7.2% on TL12 and 16.0% on JL10 over the best previously reported results, while achieving competitive performance on TE18. Furthermore, RSMBind retains predictive capability when using only pretrained RNA language model embeddings, highlighting their potential utility when explicit tertiary structural features are unavailable. Structural analysis indicates differences in prediction performance across RNA structural regions, with loop-associated binding sites generally being captured more effectively than those embedded within stem regions. Additionally, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations of selected RNA-ligand complexes provide insights into the relationship between predicted binding probabilities and dynamic ligand proximity, further highlighting the role of conformational dynamics in evaluating structure-based predictions. The source code is available at [ https://github.com/sharma-nandita/RSMBind].

items.headline: Bait: Mitigating Harmful Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Probing Reward Function
items.summary: We expose a safety vulnerability on nascent agentic reinforcement-learning-as-a-service. Specifically, with a cost as low as $20, we show that safety alignment of a large language model (e.g., Inkling) can be completely subverted through rounds of harmful agentic reinforcement learning (agentic RL) with a toxic environment from its users. We also demonstrate that upon a successful harmful agentic RL attack via the service API, the attackers can potentially use the safety-degraded model to assist with real-world harmful activities, e.g., exploit software vulnerabilities and launch code re-use attacks.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: Unfortunately, existing designs cannot accomplish security, functionality, and scalability simultaneously. They leak a certain degree of graph information, offer limited support on secure training of GNNs, and can hardly scale to large graphs. In this paper, we design and implement OblivDGL, an oblivious deep graph learning framework for secure GNN inference and training. Our design is inspired by Deep Graph Library (DGL), an industrial practice for graph learning. At its core, we distill the secure computational patterns of GNNs into a generalized form, and empower both secure GNN training and inference through a novel oblivious message passing paradigm. To realize such a paradigm, we design a new oblivious graph representation, and realize it by function secret sharing (FSS), a lightweight secure computation technique with low latency. Compared to prior secure GNN systems, OblivDGL achieves the most stringent privacy guarantees, i.e., revealing no private information except for the total number of edges and nodes. One standout feature of OblivDGL is the scalability of processing encrypted graphs by carefully tailored parallelization designs. Extensive evaluations on four benchmark graph datasets demonstrate that, compared to state-of-the-art secure GNN frameworks, OblivDGL reduces communication cost by up to 1024x and achieves up to 14.3x speedup in runtime during secure training. For secure inference, OblivDGL achieves up to 754x lower communication and a 4.19x speedup.

items.summary: In this paper, we initiate the study of multi-hop functional encryption ($\mathsf{MHFE}$), a new primitive for computing over encrypted data in recursive and multi-stage workflows while enabling controlled release of intermediate outputs. $\mathsf{MHFE}$ supports dynamic directed-acyclic computation graphs in which each node is labeled by a function and is equipped with a restricted secret key that reveals only that node's output, yet the computation can continue downstream on a forwardable encrypted state. In doing so, $\mathsf{MHFE}$ simultaneously overcomes (i) multi-hop fully homomorphic encryption's need for a globally trusted, always-online decryption key to reveal intermediate values, (ii) standard FE's lack of a native mechanism for forwarding reusable encrypted state across stages and handling evolving datasets without a fresh recomputation, and (iii) Multi Party Computation's deployment friction stemming from interaction and liveness/coordination requirements (at the cost of a central key-issuing authority).
