items.headline: A Tutorial on Oblivious Random Access Memory
items.summary: Abstract—Oblivious RAM (ORAM) is a key technique for pro- tecting memory access patterns in systems with untrusted mem- ory, including secure processors, trusted execution environments, and multi-party computation. This article presents a tutorial overview of ORAM concepts and designs from an algorithmic and cryptographic perspective. We review the security goals and threat models underlying ORAM, describe the most popular ORAM constructions and their core mechanisms, and discuss practical considerations for implementing ORAM.

items.summary: Most government transfer programs aim to target the poor. Doing so implicitly assumes that the lowest-consumption households have the highest marginal social valuation, i.e., have the highest social welfare gain from an additional dollar. But this need not be the case.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: In 600 Indonesian villages, we ask over 5,500 villagers to rank other villagers on how well off they are and how much a modest cash transfer would help them, and compare these rankings to consumption and self-assessed welfare. items.headline: Unconventional Monetary Policy and Deposit Retention -- by Philip Strahan, Tuo Yang
items.summary: The two dimensions of unconventional monetary policy — holding the short rate at the zero-lower bound (ZLB) and quantitative easing (QE) — shifted deposit composition toward more interest-sensitive customers. QE also drew rate-sensitive, large depositors from the Federal Reserve’s purchases of bonds from non-banks.

items.summary: Understanding how AI is reshaping work requires an accurate account of the tasks workers perform. Workers are often the first to see how their jobs are changing, as new responsibilities and tools often appear in everyday work before these changes reach formal descriptions. Interviews with workers can help capture these emerging changes in job tasks.

Downstream, TaskNet changes AI exposure estimates in both directions, raising them for Software Developers and Lawyers, two occupations where AI’s effects are widely debated. Because such estimates guide workforce policy and training, more complete and up-to-date task lists can help direct these efforts toward the workers most likely to be affected. TaskNet provides a foundation for keeping occupational information current and grounded in workers’ experiences as AI reshapes work.

items.summary: We estimate the maximal Sharpe ratio in large cross-sections of assets directly, without constructing the efficient portfolio. Our estimator progressively recovers this contribution, yielding tight upper and lower bounds with asymptotic confidence intervals.

items.summary: The tournament equilibrium set (TEQ), proposed by Schwartz in 1990, is a classical voting rule based on pairwise majority comparisons. Its definition is recursive: an alternative is judged by the alternatives that beat it, called its dominators, and by which of those dominators TEQ itself selects. Deciding whether a given alternative belongs to TEQ was known to be NP-hard and to lie in PSPACE.

items.headline: Physical Observables and Superselection
items.summary: It is well-known that a physical state may be represented by a unit vector in a Hilbert space, whilst a physical observable may be represented by a self-adjoint operator on that same space. However, the introduction of a superselection rule on a Hilbert space imposes constraints such that not all self-adjoint operators can represent observables, which has further consequences for the states themselves as well as the physical processes that transform them. In this article, we review the concept of superselection from the view of how such rules would affect what we consider to be physical.

items.summary: Higher-order node-based synchronization provides distinct mechanisms for discontinuous synchronization transitions. However, a comprehensive theoretical framework capable of encompassing existing models and revealing the role of higher-order interactions beyond triangles is still missing. items.headline: Tight Bounds for Downward-Closed Prophet and Secretary Problems
items.summary: We study online selection problems subject to arbitrary downward-closed feasibility constraints, under different arrival orders, with different distributional assumptions. We establish the following bounds: (1) $Θ(\log^2 n / \log \log n)$ for the standard (adversarial-order) prophet problem, (2) $Ω(\log n)$ for the (Bayesian, random-order) prophet secretary problem, and by extension, for the standard (prior-free, random-order) secretary problem, and (3) $O(\log n / \log \log n)$ for the free-order prophet problem. Together with complementary bounds established in prior work, these results pin down the asymptotically tight competitive ratios for all these variants of prophet and secretary problems subject to downward-closed constraints.

items.summary: How did mathematicians of the past relate to history? What can we learn from their experience? It is a truism to say that all people are embedded in history.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: It impacts on them in ways that they may or may not realise. At the two extremes, some may be completely oblivious; others may deliberately set out to change the historical narrative and the course of history. In this chapter, I explore these questions through two case studies. Both are of eminent British mathematicians/physicists in the late 1800s and their handling of an inverse square law of force. Both case studies show ways in which these men were blind to the history of their subject, conscious of it but limited by it, or deliberately trying to use it. First, I look at William Thomson's and James Clerk Maxwell's attempts to establish the inverse square law of electrostatics in the 1850s to 1870s. Second, I discuss John Henry Poynting and Newton's law of gravitation in the 1880s and 1890s, asking why Poynting preferred to describe his experiments as measurements of the mean density of the Earth rather than of the gravitational constant.

items.summary: Autonomous ML agents in large organizations exchange data and model outputs across organizational and legal boundaries. Which rules bind a given exchange is not fixed. items.headline: Persistent structural regimes in Bitcoin transactions relate to market cycles
items.summary: Bitcoin's blockchain is a public record of every on-chain transaction, while the price of bitcoin is set by trading on external markets. We ask whether on-chain activity alone reveals regimes associated with market trends, and whether this association remains stable over time. We summarise each week of blockchain activity from 2012 to 2026 using four measures of transaction structure and fit a two-state hidden semi-Markov model without price data.

items.headline: Scale-rich network metamaterials grow by local rules on a recursive cell division
items.summary: Scale-rich (SR) metamaterials are planar ligament networks grown by nucleating a segment at a random point and angle and extending it until it meets the existing structure. In the dual graph, where ligaments are nodes and junctions are links, the degree distribution has a $k^{-3}$ tail. We show that the SR construction is Cowan's iterated cell division with area-weighted selection, so the cell genealogy is a random binary search tree, and that the dual grows by a face-local rule: a new node joins two nodes on the boundary of one face.
